ad_hoc_blackout_authority: Securities for which Australian Ethical has received a sounding or holds information that is not in the public domain are placed on the Restricted Trading List and trading in them will not be approved; the policy does not state who administers the list or whether a person seeking approval is told that a security is on it.

rules.detail: AEI Securities are defined as 'shares or derivatives issued by' AEI, which literally covers only derivatives AEI itself issues (e.g. plan options), not a bank-written OTC put or call referencing AEI shares; if such an instrument is nonetheless treated as an AEI Security or as 'trading' in one, entering into it is a trade requiring approval under item 6's Buy/Sell AEI Securities line, subject to the Restricted Trading List and blackout period.
rules.evidence: Shares or derivatives issued by Australian Ethical Investment Limited (AEI Securities).

rules.detail: Absolute ban, no clearance route, on hedging or transferring the risk of value fluctuation of unvested equity-incentive entitlements.
rules.evidence: Any director, employee or contractor participating in an equity-based incentive plan is prohibited from entering into any transaction which would have the effect of hedging or otherwise transferring to any other person the risk of any fluctuation in the value of any unvested entitlement in AEI Securities.

rules.detail: Hedging of vested holdings is not named. Only unvested entitlement hedging is expressly banned, so a hedge over vested AEI shares is regulated (if at all) only as a general 'Buy/Sell AEI Securities' trade requiring prior approval.

rules.detail: A monetisation transferring the value-fluctuation risk of unvested entitlements is caught by the same clause that bans hedging of unvested holdings.

bespoke_clauses.clause: Shares or derivatives issued by Australian Ethical Investment Limited (AEI Securities).
bespoke_clauses.why_it_matters: The policy's core operative rules are framed around 'AEI Securities', defined as shares or derivatives issued by AEI itself; a bank-written OTC put/call is not literally 'issued by' AEI, so there is a real argument the collar derivatives fall outside the policy's scope entirely (leaving only the general insider trading law to apply), though a purposive reading would likely still treat them as regulated trading.

bespoke_clauses.clause: (no provision addresses margin loans, security, charges or secured financing anywhere in the Policy)
bespoke_clauses.why_it_matters: Granting security over vested AEI shares to fund the collar's loan leg is not listed as regulated 'Trading' and is not prohibited, restricted, or subject to any named clearance or disclosure process under this policy.

bespoke_clauses.clause: The Restricted Trading List includes any securities for which Australian Ethical has either received a sounding or has information that is not in the public domain therefore these securities will not be approved for personal trading.
bespoke_clauses.why_it_matters: Even outside a blackout period, approval for the collar could be refused without explanation if AEI shares are confidentially placed on the Restricted Trading List at the time of the request.

bespoke_clauses.clause: Where approval is granted, directors, independent committee members, employees and contractors must immediately notify, and in any event not more than 1 business day after the trade occurs, the Company Secretary (via email) of any dealings in AEI Securities.
bespoke_clauses.why_it_matters: Each leg of the collar (entry, adjustment, unwind) must be reported to the Company Secretary within 1 business day of execution.

bespoke_clauses.clause: Employees (and their close family/related persons where there is direct or indirect control over investment decisions or employee holds a beneficial interest) ... must seek approval
bespoke_clauses.why_it_matters: Routing the collar through a spouse, family trust or controlled entity does not avoid the approval requirement.

summary: A funded collar has a plausible path under this policy for vested AEI shares, but with real definitional uncertainty. Hedging is only expressly banned for unvested equity-incentive entitlements; a vested-share hedge or monetisation is not separately regulated and would, at most, need prior approval as a 'Buy/Sell AEI Securities' trade (Chair for directors/independent committee members including the CEO, or the CEO for other employees/contractors), each approval lasting 5 business days with post-trade notice to the Company Secretary within 1 business day. However, 'AEI Securities' is defined as shares or derivatives 'issued by' AEI, so a bank-written OTC put and call may arguably fall outside the policy's scope altogether rather than being expressly permitted. Critically, the policy is entirely silent on margin lending, encumbrance and secured financing, so the loan secured on the collared shares is neither prohibited nor subject to any named approval, clearance or disclosure process. The main practical constraints are the two annual blackout periods (from 1 July and 1 January until two trading days after half-year/full-year results), the discretionary Restricted Trading List, and the general ban on short-term or speculative trading.
